title: Google Commits Record $15 Billion to Finland AI Infrastructure in Largest European Bet
excerpt: The tech giant's biggest single European investment includes data centres, a 22-year nuclear power deal with Fortum, and grid upgrades — turning Finland into the 'Texas of Europe' for AI.
body:
• Google will invest at least €13 billion ($15.1 billion) in AI infrastructure in Finland through 2028, its largest single investment in any European country.
  • The deal includes a 22-year power purchase agreement with Finnish energy company Fortum, marking Google's first nuclear power deal outside the United States.
  • Fortum's stock surged 11–13% on the announcement, while Alphabet shares are up 41% over the past 12 months.
  • Finland has attracted a wave of data centre projects from Pure DC, Arcem and Nebius, earning the nickname "Texas of Europe" for its available land, ample water and advanced power grid.

Google Doubles Down on Finland

Google announced on Wednesday that it will pour at least €13 billion ($15.1 billion) into artificial intelligence infrastructure in Finland, making it the tech giant's largest single investment in a European country. The capital will be deployed through 2028 across data centres, electricity grid enhancements, clean energy projects and battery infrastructure.

"Google is proud to deepen our roots in Finland with the company's largest single investment in Europe, building on more than 15 years of sustained investment in Finland," Ruth Porat, president and chief investment officer of Alphabet and Google, said in a statement. "This investment underscores Google's commitment to grow our presence responsibly, pairing the expansion of our technical infrastructure with new energy capacity, grid enhancements, and energy affordability initiatives."

"The value of the data economy extends far beyond direct investment into spurring innovation, research, and development."

— Petteri Orpo, Prime Minister of Finland

A Nuclear-Powered AI Race

Central to the deal is a 22-year life-extension power purchase agreement with Fortum, Finland's largest energy company, which operates the Loviisa nuclear power plant in southern Finland. The agreement marks Google's first nuclear power arrangement outside the United States, signalling that the global race to build increasingly powerful AI systems is no longer centred solely on software — it is increasingly a competition for reliable energy, computing power and land.

Fortum's stock jumped 11–13% on the news. The two companies also plan to "work to identify new business models to improve the commercial viability of potential new nuclear reactors" at a site in southern Finland, according to the announcement.

Why Finland Is Becoming the 'Texas of Europe'

Finland has emerged as a magnet for hyperscalers and AI developers seeking locations that can support enormous energy demands. The country offers relatively abundant low-carbon electricity — including nuclear power — available land, ample water for cooling, and an advanced power grid. These advantages are in short supply across most of Europe, where energy often has to be imported.

Several major data centre projects have been announced in Finland in recent months. Pure DC committed €1.5 billion to build a 110-megawatt campus with the potential to scale beyond 550 megawatts. Arcem has plans for a site with up to 500 megawatts capacity. And in March, Nebius unveiled plans to build one of Europe's largest AI factories in the country.

What This Means for the Tech Industry

Google's Finland investment comes at a time when the AI infrastructure buildout is accelerating globally, with hyperscalers committing tens of billions to secure the compute and energy resources needed to train and deploy next-generation models. For the Indian tech ecosystem — which supplies a significant share of the talent and services powering these data centre operations — the scale of European AI investment signals sustained demand for cloud engineering, infrastructure management and AI development skills.

Alphabet shares have risen 41% over the past 12 months to trade at $338.36, reflecting investor confidence in the company's AI strategy. The Finland announcement deepens Google's commitment to a region that is fast becoming Europe's primary AI infrastructure corridor.

Looking Ahead

The investment will run through 2028, with Google expected to announce specific data centre locations and construction timelines in the coming months. The nuclear power partnership with Fortum could also serve as a template for similar deals in other energy-constrained markets, as tech companies increasingly recognise that the AI arms race is, at its core, an energy race.
